e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Benaiah.” It identifies a particular man rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. The name appears 42 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Kings and Chronicles, and it is consistently rendered “Benaiah.” Its occurrences include references to him among David’s mighty men and in the royal events surrounding David’s succession. Because it functions as a personal name, the surrounding verse is needed to identify which mention or role is intended.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “Berothite,” a designation identifying a person by connection with Beroth. It functions as a personal identifying term rather than as an action, quality, or object. This word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 11:39. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, the word itself supports the identification but does not establish additional details about the person or the role he plays there.

e.t: This Hebrew verb expresses willingness—the act of agreeing to do something or allowing it to happen. It describes a person’s readiness or consent rather than merely an outward action. In the Old Testament, it occurs 54 times, so its sense is used across a range of situations involving whether someone will accept, permit, or choose a course of action. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains being willing or consenting.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “valley,” referring to a low area of land between hills or mountains. It is used for named and recognizable places as well as for valleys described in journeys, battles, boundaries, and other events. The word occurs 61 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it commonly identifies physical landscape rather than expressing an abstract idea. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding place names and actions connected with the valley.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “together.” It functions as the sentence’s predicate, describing how something is joined or arranged in relation to something else. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in 2 Kings 2:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence and its subject and object, but the available rendering presents the central idea clearly: together. The word is therefore concerned with a relationship or action involving things brought into a shared arrangement.

carry away, × indeed, secretly bring, steal (away), get by stealth.
d: to thieve (literally or figuratively); by implication, to deceive

e.t: This Hebrew word means “steal.” It describes the act of taking another person’s property or possession. In the Old Testament, it is used as a verbal action, presenting stealing as something a person does. The word occurs 40 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing across laws, narratives, wisdom sayings, and prophetic writing. Its central idea remains consistent: wrongful taking is identified as stealing, whether the subject is a person or an object of concern.

This Hebrew word refers to bees, the stinging insects known for swarming and pursuing others. It is a noun used in the Old Testament for the creatures themselves rather than for an abstract idea. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy, Judges, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its repeated rendering as “bees” supports this straightforward meaning, while the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on their presence, swarm, or threatening pursuit.

This Hebrew verb describes an action, but its ordinary English meaning cannot be determined confidently from the available information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Nahum 3:2, and the verse text is not available here. Its role is identified as a predicate in relationships connected with that verse, but those links do not establish a precise definition without the surrounding wording.

e.t: This word functions as “of,” marking a relationship between one thing and another in a phrase. In its Hebrew corpus, it appears three times, all in Ezra. It is therefore a connecting word rather than a complete statement by itself. Its precise contribution in any sentence comes from the surrounding words, but its basic role is to link related terms.

This word is the personal name “Darda.” It refers to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 4:31, and the English rendering preserves it as “Darda.” Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes this person from others mentioned in the passage. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

e.t: Hodaviah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Hodaviah.” It identifies people rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The name appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus: three times in 1 Chronicles and once in Ezra. Because no explanatory definition is attached to the name, its basic use is as a person’s designation. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which Hodaviah is meant in each occurrence.

The surrounding evidence presents Hillel as a person connected with the events recorded there, including his death and burial. Because the actual verse text is not included here, the name itself should be understood simply as a personal designation; its precise role in each passage depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: “Zebah” is a personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than as a description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs 12 times, concentrated mainly in Judges 8, with one occurrence in Psalms. The available biblical renderings consistently preserve it as “Zebah,” so it should be read as a name in these passages, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific role and actions.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “removed.” It describes people being taken away or separated from their place among others. In its seven Old Testament occurrences, it functions as a term for this outcome rather than naming a person or object. The word appears especially in Jeremiah, where it is applied repeatedly to those separated from their land and community. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its basic sense is “time”. It refers to time as a recognized period or span. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears eleven times, showing its recurring use for speaking about time across different passages. The surrounding words determine the precise way that period is understood in each sentence.

Hushah is a personal name, referring to an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:4, and the English Bible renders it as “Hushah.” Because this word functions as a name rather than a common noun or action word, the name itself does not provide a broader everyday definition. Its precise significance in that genealogy depends on the surrounding verse and family record, but its basic lexical role is to identify Hushah as a person.

gl: to broaden out the ear (with the hand), i.e. (by implication) to listen
give (perceive by the) ear, hear(-ken). See 239 .
d: to broaden out the ear (with the hand), i.e. (by implication) to listen

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the “ear,” especially as the part of a person that receives spoken words and gives attention to what is heard. It can therefore function in expressions that call someone to attend carefully to speech or instruction. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 41 times, appearing from Genesis through Joel. Its use is associated with hearing God, prophets, and other speakers, as well as with calls for people to give careful attention.

The Hebrew word means “engraved.” It describes something marked into a surface rather than merely placed upon it, functioning as a descriptive term for a fixed inscription or carving. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at Exodus 32:16, so its ordinary meaning is supported by this single occurrence. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain its specific force there rather than make a broader contextual claim about the word.

The name appears 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including accounts and genealogical records. In genealogical passages, Ahitub is connected with family lines through birth and descent. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its normal function is simply to name this individual.

This Hebrew word refers to fasting, the practice of going without food. It functions as a noun describing that practice rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 6:18. The word’s basic meaning is therefore focused and specific: it identifies fasting itself. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the particular significance of fasting in that occurrence.

e.t: Jehdeiah is a Hebrew personal name rather than a common word with a stated descriptive meaning. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles. The available information identifies the name and its occurrences but does not provide a definition or explanation of its underlying name meaning. Therefore, it is best understood as the name of an individual, not as a word describing an action, quality, or object.

This Hebrew word refers to a “gathering,” describing people coming together as a group. It functions as a noun rather than an action word or personal name. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Genesis 49:10 and once in Proverbs 30:17. Those occurrences show that the word can describe a gathered group or assembly, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force in each passage.

gl: convenient, equity, Jasher, just, meet(-est), pleased well right(-eous), straight, (most) upright(-ly, -ness).

e.t: This Hebrew word means “right,” describing what is straight, proper, or morally upright. It can characterize a person, conduct, judgment, or way that conforms to what is good and fitting. In English Bible renderings, it is also represented by “well,” showing that the word may describe something done appropriately or correctly, not merely a physical direction. It occurs 119 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is a recurring word for integrity and what accords with the right standard.

gl: Elim , a place in the Desert
d: Elim , a place in the Desert

e.t: Elim is a Hebrew place name, referring to a location in the Israelites’ journey. It is not presented here as a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but as the name of a particular place. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in four verses: Exodus 15:27, Exodus 16:1, and Numbers 33:9–10. Its precise significance in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and journey account.

Its use reaches from creation passages to descriptions of the cherubim and other settings where wings are mentioned. e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to the “heart,” the inner center from which a person thinks, desires, chooses, and responds. It is used in connection with attention to God’s commands, faithful action, wisdom, and generosity. Thus, the heart describes a person’s inward life and will, not merely passing emotion. This Old Testament word occurs 252 times, showing its broad importance in describing human devotion and conduct. e.t: This Hebrew noun means “razor,” an instrument used to cut or shave hair. It appears three times in the Old Testament, including passages concerning a person’s hair and a vow involving hair. The word therefore names the tool itself, rather than the act of shaving or the hair being cut. Its use in Judges and 1 Samuel consistently points to a physical razor.

This Hebrew word means “if,” introducing a condition or imagined possibility. It connects one circumstance with what may follow from it, helping a sentence express uncertainty, qualification, or a hypothetical situation. It is a conjunction rather than a name for a person, object, or action. This word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once in Esther and once in Ecclesiastes. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary function is to frame something as conditional or possible.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “tribute”—something set apart and given as an offering or required contribution. In its six Old Testament occurrences, it appears in Numbers 31, where the tribute is associated with counted spoils and with giving according to a command. Its use presents the tribute as a defined portion that belongs to the Lord and is transferred to him through the appointed arrangement.

gl: × ought, (that which cometh of) sale, that which...sold, ware.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to something “sold.” It identifies what is involved in being sold rather than expressing the action as a verb. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs 10 times, with most occurrences in Leviticus 25 and additional occurrences in Deuteronomy, Nehemiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the way the sentence presents what was sold.

Muppim is a Hebrew personal name, preserved in English as “Muppim.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Genesis 46:21. Its precise significance is not defined by the name itself; the surrounding verse is needed to identify the person and explain his place in that passage.

gl: to polish ; by implication, to make bald (the head), to gall (the shoulder); also, to sharpen
bright, furbish, (have his) hair (be) fallen off, peeled, pluck off (hair).
d: to polish ; by implication, to make bald (the head), to gall (the shoulder); also, to sharpen

e.t: This Hebrew word describes hair being removed or plucked, and can also refer to the hair itself in contexts describing its loss. Its ordinary sense centers on plucking or stripping hair away rather than merely cutting it. It occurs 12 times in the Old Testament, including passages rendered “hair” and “plucked.” The precise force in any verse depends on whether the sentence emphasizes the hair or the act of removing it.

This Hebrew word refers to “desolations”—places or conditions left ruined and empty. It is used twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Psalms. As a noun-like expression, it points to places or conditions rather than to an action, person, or emotion. Because it appears in only two verses and no surrounding passage is provided here, its precise force in each verse must be understood from that passage’s context.

Nebai is a Hebrew personal name preserved in English Bible translations. In the Hebrew corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah 10:19, referring to the same named individual in that verse. The available wording supports the name “Nebai,” but does not provide an additional dictionary meaning or description. Its precise significance therefore comes from the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Netaim is a Hebrew name used once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:23.
